name: Clomiphene / enclomiphene
lead: Clomiphene (clomifene, brand Clomid) is an oral selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved for treating ovulatory dysfunction in women [1][2]. In men it is used off-label to raise the body's own testosterone, and it is discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities as a way to do this without testosterone injections or to restart the axis after steroid cycles [3].

Clomiphene is a mixture of roughly 62 percent enclomiphene and 38 percent zuclomiphene isomers [1]. Enclomiphene, the more antiestrogenic isomer, was developed as a purified drug for men with secondary hypogonadism, but regulatory approval was not obtained and development was discontinued in 2021 [4].

Trials in hypogonadal men report raised testosterone [1][4]. Reported adverse effects include visual symptoms, and the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits clomiphene [1][2]. No published trial was found testing it for facial or appearance outcomes.

paras: The US label states clomiphene citrate is indicated for ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy, including those with polycystic ovary syndrome [2]. Randomized trials have compared it with metformin and letrozole for infertility in PCOS [5][6]. In men it is sometimes used as an alternative to testosterone replacement for hypogonadism, roughly doubling to 2.5-fold testosterone levels, and has also been used for gynecomastia, though it is not recommended for it [1].

On looksmax.org, users discuss enclomiphene as a way to increase testosterone and as an add-on in steroid or other compound regimens, and some posters cite a 2024 study comparing clomiphene and enclomiphene as showing larger testosterone increases and fewer side effects for enclomiphene [3]. This is a user report; the study itself was not among the sources reviewed.

Clomiphene blocks estrogen's negative feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH pulses and raising LH and FSH, which stimulates ovulation in women and testicular testosterone production in men [1]. It is a prodrug whose active metabolites form via CYP2D6 [1]. Enclomiphene is described as pro-androgenic and zuclomiphene as pro-estrogenic with a half-life of days to a week [1]. Enclomiphene raises total and free testosterone without a disproportionate rise in DHT [4].

In the US label's clinical-trial data, ovarian enlargement (13.6 percent) and vasomotor flushes (10.4 percent) were most common; visual symptoms including blurring and scotomata occasionally occur and increase with total dose or duration, and may rarely be prolonged or irreversible [2]. Use in pregnancy is contraindicated [2]. Other reports include liver abnormalities and rare hepatotoxicity [1].
For enclomiphene, pooled data from 1,403 trial participants reported headache, hot flush, nausea and rarer thromboembolic events, as summarized in a reference article [4].

Clomiphene was synthesized in 1956 by a team led by Frank Palopoli at William S. Merrell Chemical Company, patented in 1959, and approved in the US in 1967 as Clomid [1]. It was studied for breast cancer from 1964 to 1974 and abandoned for that use [1]. Enclomiphene (Androxal, EnCyzix) was pursued for male hypogonadism; in January 2018 the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorization, and development was discontinued in April 2021 [4].

Clomiphene is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia [1]. WADA prohibits it (category S4), and it can be an undeclared ingredient in black-market products; athletes have also tested positive via contaminated food [1].

Registered phase 3 trials include enclomiphene in men with secondary hypogonadism (n=104, n=300 extension, and n=499 safety study) [7][8][9]. A published account reports testosterone rises in hypogonadal men on clomiphene, from about 309 to 642 ng/dL in one study [1]. Large trials in women include NEJM comparisons of clomiphene with metformin and with letrozole for PCOS infertility [5][6]. No studies were found of either drug for facial appearance.

lore.intro: Clomiphene and enclomiphene are discussed as ways to boost endogenous testosterone and as post-cycle options.

claims.claim: Enclomiphene raises testosterone more than clomiphene with fewer side effects
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster cited a September 2024 comparison as showing enclomiphene boosted testosterone more with fewer side effects, and another user called it a solid add-on to other compound regimens [3].
claims.experts: Reference sources describe enclomiphene as the more androgenic isomer reported to be about twice as effective as the mixture, while zuclomiphene is pro-estrogenic [1]; it was not approved by regulators [4].

claims.claim: These drugs raise testosterone without testosterone replacement
claims.believers: Users describe them as stimulating the body's own production.
claims.experts: Trials and reviews report increased testosterone and preserved sperm counts in men with secondary hypogonadism [4]; clomiphene is off-label for men [1].

card.summary: A fertility SERM used off-label by men to raise their own testosterone; trial data in hypogonadal men, none for looks.
card.note: Prescription-only; visual disturbances reported; WADA-prohibited; enclomiphene never approved.

quick.overview:
Clomiphene is an oral fertility drug that men also use off-label to raise their own testosterone. Enclomiphene is its more androgenic isomer.

Trials in men with secondary hypogonadism report testosterone rises. No studies were found on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks estrogen feedback in the brain, increasing LH and FSH signals that drive testicular testosterone production.
quick.risks: The label lists ovarian enlargement and flushes in women, and visual symptoms that can occasionally be prolonged. Enclomiphene was refused EU authorization in 2018. Clomiphene is prescription-only and WADA-prohibited.
